cim_eredeti: Healthcare still playing catchup in industrial AI marathon
szoveg_eredeti:
A new study confirms that healthcare workers still use AI less often than workers in other large economic sectors, lagging behind not only the perennial “league leader,” information technology, but also financial services, manufacturing, retail and education.

The new findings do not differentiate between clinical and administrative occupations, instead grouping all as, simply, “healthcare workers.”

Still, the study helpfully shows that healthcare as a whole has far to go before it’s considered a competitively AI-rich field to work in, do business with or receive services from.

For the study, published Nov. 25 in JAMA Health Forum, Harvard healthcare researchers led by Rosemary Martoma, MD, MBChB, analyzed data from the March 2026 U.S. Census Bureau Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS).

The study sample reflected input from more than 6,200 earners who worked the week prior to receiving the survey.

Tabulating the results, Martoma and colleagues found that, overall, 32% of healthcare workers vs. 41% of non-healthcare workers had used AI at work during the prior week.

Further, fewer than 10% of healthcare workers, 8.3%, had used AI daily over the prior week, while 14.6% of non-healthcare workers had done so.

The survey named 11 tasks doable with AI. Some of the largest gaps between healthcare and non-healthcare uses turned up for:

In their discussion, Martoma and colleagues note the 51.8% unadjusted prevalence among workers in healthcare occupations that they found was below the 54% to 72% reported in recent physician surveys, most of which have sampled single professions through nonprobability panels.

“Differences may reflect broader occupational coverage and different sampling and measurement approaches,” the authors remark. “Given that the largest use gaps involved administrative and information-processing tasks, they may represent missed opportunities to reduce workload, although HTOPS did not assess objective productivity or care outcomes.”

Federal surveys need more granular occupational measures, they add, to identify which healthcare roles account for this gap.

Dave P. has worked in journalism, marketing and public relations for more than 30 years, frequently concentrating on hospitals, healthcare technology and Catholic communications. He has also specialized in fundraising communications, ghostwriting for CEOs of local, national and global charities, nonprofits and foundations.
